_about: The How to Play page (js/ui/help.js). Plain-English summary of docs/RULES.md for players: if a rule changes there, change it here too. Each section has a title and paragraphs; 'diagram': 'lane' draws the small picture of which territories touch. See docs/DATA.md.
title: How to play
intro: Each turn is one month, from December 1914 to November 1918. In your turn you give orders (moves and attacks together), they appear as pencil arrows, and nothing happens until you tap COMMIT. You play on the board: one square per territory. The Map button shows the same war on the real map.

sections.title: A month of the war
paragraphs: 1. Events and reinforcements arrive. 2. The War Office budget: Industry buys shells and research (done for you unless you turn Auto-allocate off in the menu (top left)). 3. The German turn: moves, then attacks. 4. The Entente turn: moves, then attacks. 5. Supply, digging in, replacements and National Will happen by themselves.
The line under the date always says what you can do now, and what you have left to spend.

sections.title: Moving: road and rail
paragraphs: Road: a unit moves up to 2 territories, each step to a neighbour that shares a side (not corner to corner), and only through your own territory. Tap the unit, then a territory outlined in brass.

Rail: a unit can go any distance through a chain of your own territory. Tap a territory outlined in blue dashes. Each month Germany has 3 rail moves, France 2 and Britain 1. A unit that goes by rail can't attack that month, so use rail to fill gaps and bring up reserves, not to attack straight away.
Each unit moves once a month. At most 3 units can stand in one territory. You never move into enemy territory: you take it by attacking.

sections.title: Splitting and merging pieces
paragraphs: In your turn you can split a piece: tap it, then 'Split off 1 step' (or 2, or 3). The new, smaller piece stays in the territory and can move on its own. Use it to leave a small picket in a quiet sector and march the rest to where the attack will be.

Two pieces of the same nation and type in one territory can merge back into one if their steps fit (4 for infantry). The merged piece takes the lower quality. The computer merges its damaged pieces but never splits.
Don't leave a territory empty: an empty territory is taken without a fight. Even a 1-step picket makes the enemy pay an attack for it.

sections.title: Who can attack whom
paragraphs: A unit can attack an enemy territory that shares a side with the territory it stands in once its moves are done. Tap the unit: the enemy territories it can attack are outlined in red. If it has to step up first, tapping the red territory orders that road move for you, then opens the attack. Each unit attacks once a month, must be in supply, and must not have come by rail.
An attack costs 1 Offensive Point (2 if units of two nations attack together).

Each enemy front-line territory touches only one of yours, straight across no-man's-land. So the way to attack is to bring up to 3 units into one front territory, then attack from it, all in the same turn. One unit against one dug-in unit almost never wins.

sections.title: Odds and dice
paragraphs: Odds: your steps against theirs give a column: 1:2, 1:1, 3:2, 2:1, 3:1 or 4:1. Below 1:2 you can't attack.

Shifts then move the column: −1 for each trench level, −1 or −2 for hard ground (ridges, forest, mountains, fortresses, the flooded Yser, autumn mud in Flanders), −1 in winter (December to February), +1 for each munition in a barrage (up to 2, or 3 from June 1916), and the nations' strengths.

Then two dice are rolled. The result says how many steps each side loses, and on good rolls an R: the defenders retreat and you take the territory. The chance of an R is 0, 3, 17, 42, 58 or 83% from 1:2 to 4:1. That's why the odds jump in steps.

Dug in: from trench level 2, an R becomes one more loss instead of a retreat. Then you only take the territory by destroying every defending step, which is why a well-held trench can show 0%: wear it down over several months, or attack somewhere weaker.

A failed attack at 1:1 or worse costs your nation 3 National Will. The order slip shows the roll you need, what every roll would do, and why the odds are what they are. BEST ATTACKS shows your three best chances this turn.

sections.title: After a battle
paragraphs: Losses come off the strongest unit first. A unit at 0 steps is destroyed (it can be rebuilt later with Manpower).

If the territory falls, the defenders fall back one territory deeper into their own lines (or are destroyed if there's no room), up to 2 of your attackers move in, the territory becomes yours and its trench drops to 0.
After each turn plays back, the panel shows a battle report for every attack: the dice, the losses, who fell back, who advanced and whether the front line moved.

sections.title: Supply
paragraphs: A unit is in supply if a chain of your own territory leads back to your rear line (British units: to the Channel Ports or Hazebrouck). A unit out of supply can't attack and loses 1 step a month. Don't let a salient get cut off.

sections.title: The War Office budget
paragraphs: Manpower goes to replacements by itself: 1 Manpower adds a step to a damaged unit, 2 rebuild a destroyed one.

Industry buys munitions (1 each) for the stockpile, which holds at most 3 and carries over, or goes into research to bring a new weapon or tactic before its historical date. Unspent Industry is lost. Auto-allocate starts on and does this for you. Turn it off in the menu (top left) to choose yourself: the budget page then appears in months when there's research to pick.

sections.title: How to win
paragraphs: Every nation has National Will. It falls with losses, lost cities, failed attacks and hunger at home. Germany wins at once if France's or Britain's Will reaches 0 or it takes Paris; the Entente wins at once if Germany's Will reaches 0.

Otherwise the war ends in November 1918 and the Armistice Score decides: German Will minus the average of French and British Will, plus the value of cities taken. Sitting still loses: the blockade and the Americans wear Germany down. Reckless attacks lose too.
